title: One sentence of policy: the exception and the ghost of Annex A
paras: Rural workers' dwellings, and it starts with one sentence of policy. National policy says avoid isolated homes in the countryside, except where there's an essential need for a rural worker to live at or near their work, and that expressly includes someone taking majority control of a farm business. The written guide has the paragraph number. Notice what's not there: no functional test, no financial test, no three-year profitability rule, no definition of essential. It leaves the assessment to the authority, and that silence is the whole difficulty.

The detail used to live elsewhere: a chain of old guidance, a circular then two annexes, setting out a structured test of functional need, financial viability and a standard occupancy condition. In 2012 the first Framework replaced something like a thousand pages of it with one short document. The detail didn't survive; the expectations of decision-makers largely did.

That old test, Annex A, is still the spine of every assessment. For a permanent dwelling on an established unit: a clearly established functional need for a full-time worker; the unit established at least three years, profitable for at least one, and financially sound with a clear prospect of continuing; a need not capable of being met by another dwelling on the unit or other suitable accommodation in the area; and ordinary planning requirements satisfied. A new enterprise took the temporary route. Every limb survives today.

The twist is that the Framework's silence left a vacuum, and authorities filled it with the guidance just withdrawn, local plans reproducing the old tests word for word and so giving them fresh statutory footing, others applying Annex A out of habit. But the modern wording is wider two ways: rural worker reaches beyond agriculture and forestry to equestrian and other land-based enterprises; and majority control names the succession case directly, once argued the hard way through the functional test.

title: Functional need: essential, not convenient
paras: Functional need, essential, not convenient. Everything turns on one question: is it essential for the proper functioning of the enterprise that a worker is at or near the site? Yes, you've got a foundation; no, nothing else saves it. The old guidance put it in words nobody's bettered: is it essential for a worker to be readily available at most times, because animals or processes need essential care at short notice, or to deal with emergencies that could cause serious loss, like frost damage or failed automatic systems.

Two phrases carry the weight. Readily available at most times isn't met by a worker being busy, working long hours, or rarely off the holding, a nine-to-five operation, however demanding, doesn't generate the need. At short notice means delay causes real harm; if it can wait until morning, the case weakens. Hence the contrast: a dairy herd is milked morning and night, calving much of the year, a cow in difficulty needs help within the hour, while the arable farm next door grows unsupervised, its damage done whether anyone's there or not. The worker has to be within sight and sound of the enterprise, which ties the functional case to siting.

The boundaries are precise. Welfare drives the strongest livestock cases, calving, farrowing, lambing, stock ill or cast at any hour. But the version that any farm with animals needs a dwelling is resisted, plenty run without every worker resident, and fattening cattle are finished in open yards. Security helps on remote holdings with genuine crime but won't justify a dwelling on its own, though it can inform siting, since a house by the entrance controls the access. A need from processing or manufacturing, not the farming itself, doesn't support an agricultural dwelling. And the need belongs to the enterprise, not the applicant, the same need whoever does the work.

You assess it as the enterprise runs now. An established need supports a permanent dwelling; a prospective one, the herd still building, points to the temporary route. Change is the classic driver: livestock brought onto an arable holding, the Embleton situation; expansion carrying the labour requirement over the full-time threshold; a change of system, outdoor stock brought in or breeding added to fattening; or an owner who, through age or ill health, can't do work that still has to be done. But the change must have an agricultural purpose of its own, and must actually have happened, stock on the ground with numbers and dates, buildings in use, records, not intentions.

title: Measuring the enterprise: the Standard Labour Requirement
paras: Measuring the enterprise, the Standard Labour Requirement. The functional test says whether an enterprise needs a worker at all; the labour requirement says whether it's big enough for that need to be real rather than notional. You list every class of stock by head and every crop and grassland type by the hectare, accurately, because the inputs must reconcile with the holding's records, accounts and subsidy returns, then multiply each by the published standard figure and total the hours. The recognised datasets are the Nix pocketbook, the S-A-C figures and the Costing Book, with DEFRA's Farm Business Survey as an independent check.

Then add for overheads, usually ten per cent, up to twenty depending on the enterprises, applied once, and divide by the productive hours one full-time worker gives in a year. That divisor sits below contracted hours, for holidays, sickness and unproductive time; around two thousand two hundred is common, but justify yours, a low one reports more units off the same holding. Run it for each dataset and take a reasoned average.

The contrast shows why it's powerful. A three-hundred-and-sixty-five-acre dairy holding carrying three hundred and sixty-five cows, with followers, comes out around ten and a quarter units on the Costing Book, eight and a fifth on S-A-C, seven on Nix, an average of eight and a half, with the Farm Business Survey almost exactly there. The identical land in winter wheat, barley and oilseed rape comes out under one, not even a single full-time job. Same acres, a labour requirement differing by a factor of about nine.

But the figure measures labour consumed, not houses justified. A requirement of eight doesn't mean eight dwellings, much of that labour can travel in; it's the functional test that governs how many workers must be resident. A first dwelling needs a requirement above one; two doesn't get you two dwellings; a second only becomes arguable as it approaches or passes three. Alongside it, run livestock units and stocking density, the dairy example carries around four hundred and twenty-four units, about two-point-nine per hectare, to confirm the stock can be carried on the land, your check against inflated numbers.

title: The financial position and the viability myth
paras: The financial position, and the viability myth. There's no financial viability test for a permanent rural worker's dwelling under the Framework. Yet applicants still lead with accounts and officers still demand them, both working from a test that no longer exists. Two questions get muddled, does the work need a worker on the land, and does the farm turn a profit, and only the first is the test. A holding can show a clear need and run at break-even, or at a loss in a bad year, and still justify a dwelling; a profitable enterprise with no need won't. The habit is a leftover from Annex A, whose sound-financial-basis and viability limbs were hard tests for years and weren't carried into the Framework in 2012. The policy didn't soften the test; it dropped it.

The courts were uneasy with mechanical financial tests even before that. In Petter, the Court of Appeal quashed a refusal of temporary permission where the inspector accepted the functional need but refused because profit fell below the agricultural minimum wage. A financial test was only ever a means to an end, to stop bogus applications and give assurance the farming would continue, and on a subsistence holding profitability told you nothing about whether it was genuine or would last. So Petter is your authority against a crude profit test.

The Framework question got answered in Embleton, where the challenge was that viability was implicit in the isolated-homes exception. The judge rejected it: the Framework asks only whether the enterprise has an essential need for a worker there or near there. Three things temper the weight though, it's a deputy High Court decision, it arose on a temporary dwelling, and its reasoning sits in tension with Redhill Aerodrome, where the Court of Appeal wouldn't read the Framework's brevity as silently abandoning the old policy. Followed consistently, but not bulletproof.

So money still matters, twice over. First, financial evidence goes to whether the farming is real and will carry on, stock and cropping records, sale receipts, subsidy claims, accounts as proof of a genuine business, not a profit figure marked pass or fail, and money spent on buildings, services or fencing shows real commitment. The sound-financial-basis expectation does survive for temporary dwellings for new enterprises, where a business plan is still looked for. Second, if the local plan carries a financial test, that's part of the development plan and no dead letter, but the argument runs: the plan has primacy; Embleton supplies the material consideration that national policy has no viability test; and cases like City of Edinburgh and Hopkins Homes give the principle that a policy outdated by a change in national policy gets reduced weight. So you argue little weight attaches, never that it's void.

title: Suitable and available accommodation
paras: Suitable and available accommodation. Functional need gets you to the starting line, but this question defeats more applications than any other. If a suitable dwelling already exists, or is available nearby, the essential need is met without building, and the justification falls away. Two separate limbs. Suitable means fit to meet the particular need, so not a dwelling miles from the stock, whatever its state, nor one too small for the household, too costly to run on an agricultural wage, or unable to give close supervision. Available means available in fact, not merely in existence, so not a house someone else occupies, not for sale or let, or priced beyond the worker who must live in it. Running the two together is a common error, and it cuts both ways.

The leading case is Keen. Functional need for a resident stockman was accepted, but permission was refused on the footing that the applicant's own family home nearby could be shared at the critical times, even though that might cause substantial inconvenience and financial loss. The court quashed it: availability and suitability must be scrutinised, not assumed from mere existence, the real questions being whether the house is available in fact, what competing demands are on it, and whether a family can be expected to move out or a home be carved up at all. Someone who's established a need can't be made to give up his own home.

Cussons drove the same point home. Three alternatives were offered and all three failed for one reason: a house that could take the worker but was never tested and stopped working once the senior partner's health failed; a building offered as temporary against many months of calving; and a farmhouse that might be bought or rented from an owner who might do neither. A possibility isn't availability; an alternative that exists only after works, consents or someone else's cooperation isn't, without more, available.

Three scenarios recur. First, the dwelling sold away from the holding, the severance problem: the authority asks why a new house should replace one voluntarily given up, but the sold-off house is almost always in separate ownership, occupied, not for sale, and often no longer suitable anyway, and the closer the sale to the application, the sharper the scrutiny. Second, a dwelling already tied by an occupancy condition, which defeats you only if it's suitable and available to the present need, a tied house occupied by another agricultural or retired worker isn't available on demand, and one tied cottage doesn't cap a holding whose need has genuinely grown. And third, open-market houses, usually unsuitable by distance, since a house two miles off can't serve a need defined by sight and sound, and unavailable by price, since open-market value is beyond an agricultural wage, which is why the tied dwelling the policy contemplates is a modest one.

title: Temporary dwellings and the occupancy tie
paras: Temporary dwellings, and the occupancy tie. A new or expanding enterprise whose need is only prospective takes the temporary route, typically a caravan for three years, modest and removable so it comes off if the case is never made out. Three things carry it: a credible prospect the functional need will arise, shown by a projected labour requirement worked with the same rigour as a present one; a firm intention and reasonable likelihood the enterprise will develop as planned, the surviving role of the business plan, telling a genuine proposal from a lifestyle project; and the absence of suitable available accommodation, tested now, not deferred. The period tests permanence rather than viability, and land tenure feeds that: a wholly owned holding reads as permanent, one on farm business tenancies less so, one on annually licensed land least of all, because if the land goes, the stock go, and the need evaporates.

The period ends one of three ways. Either the need has become established, stock on the ground and the labour requirement over the threshold, and the permanent application is judged on the position as it stands, the functional test applied afresh and more demandingly, because a temporary consent is no promise of a permanent one. Or it hasn't, and the accommodation comes off and the land is restored. Or it's unresolved and a further period sought, and these aren't freely renewable, repeated extensions were treated as unsatisfactory as far back as Petter, because an endless run would collapse the distinction and secure permanent occupation by the back door. An applicant at three years still relying on what the enterprise will become has usually run out of road.

A permitted dwelling carries the occupancy condition. The standard form, essentially unchanged since 1973, limits occupation to someone solely or mainly employed, or last employed, in agriculture or forestry in the locality, plus a surviving spouse or civil partner and resident dependants. Notice it doesn't tie occupation to the particular holding: a worker on another farm, a local contractor, a retired worker all qualify, which weakens any argument that no occupier could be found. The suppressed value is the whole point, keeping the dwelling affordable to the workers it exists to house, and the gap between tied and untied value is what every removal fight is about. Survivor protection is personal: when the surviving partner dies or leaves, the condition revives in full.

Removal runs two routes. First, by application to vary the condition, giving a fresh permission judged against current policy, on the ground it's no longer necessary, proved above all by marketing: the dwelling genuinely offered to qualifying occupiers through channels they'd actually see, at a price reflecting the tie, the discount a matter of valuation evidence with figures around a third often cited, over a sustained period, commonly about twelve months, with no qualifying interest coming forward. Arguing only that the original holding has gone fails, because the tie is to agriculture in the locality. Second, by time: ten years' continuous breach by a non-qualifying occupier gives immunity, confirmed by certificate, the burden on the owner on the balance of probabilities, and any period of compliant occupation, including by a qualifying survivor, resets the clock. That ten-year period wasn't touched by the 2024 enforcement reforms. And check the instrument, a pre-1973 condition may be imprecise enough to challenge, and some ties are planning obligations tying the dwelling to the land rather than dictating who lives there, with a different route for modification.
